# 2.5 - Inputs and Outputs of Functions {.unnumbered}

So far in this unit, you’ve learned how to evaluate expressions by plugging in values for variables. You’ve also simplified expressions using distribution and by combining like terms. In this lesson, we will use those same skills in a new way.

Picture a small mystery machine on a desk with a sign that says “Feed me.” On the machine is a big letter "f" and on the table are number cards. You slide a 5 into the top, and out comes 13. You try 7, and out comes 17. When you feed the same number again, you get the same result again. The machine always behaves the same way.

What could the machine be doing to the numbers? How could we describe that process so someone else could use it too? Machines like this, where each input leads to one specific output, are called {{< glink slug=function text=functions >}}.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I can read and use function notation like $f(x) = 2x+3$.
- [ ] I can evaluate a function for a given input by substituting and simplifying.
- [ ] I can simplify a function rule using distribution and combining like terms.
- [ ] I can identify whether a relation is a function based on input and output pairs.
:::

2. Simplify $3(x+4) - 2(3x - 1)$.

3. What rule could explain how to get the outputs in the table from the inputs?

{{< learn >}}

### 2.5.1 - What Is Function Notation?

Imagine our “mystery machine” from the introduction.

![The mystery machine](/images/Unit_2/Lesson_5/function_machine.png){width="50%"}

Did you figure out what rule the machine is following? With only two examples, we can't be 100% sure, but from the examples we have (5 → 13, 7 → 17), one possible rule is: “double the input and then add 3”.

In algebra, we name the machine and write its rule using function notation.

$$
f(x) = 2x+3
$$

* $f$ is the name of the function (we also use $g$, $h$, etc.).
* $f(x)$ (read "f of x") means $x$ is the input variable.
* $2x + 3$ is the rule for the output. It tells what to do to $x$.

:::{.gotcha title="$f(x)$ is not $f$ times $x$."}
Read $f(x)$ as “$f$ of $x$.” It is a single name for the output when the input is $x$. It does **not** mean to multiply $f$ and $x$.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Describe in words what $g(y) = 2y - 2$ does."}
It takes the input $y$, doubles it, and subtracts 2.

**Example:** $g(3) = 2(3)-2 = 4$
:::

***

### 2.5.2 - Is It a Function? (Using Tables)

A **relation** is any set of input-output pairs. A **function** is a special kind of relation: **each input has exactly one output**.

We can check this quickly with an input/output table.

**How to check a table**

1. **Scan the input column.**
   If the **same input** appears with **two different outputs**, it is **not** a function.

2. **Repeated input is okay if the output is the same.**
   If an input repeats but the output matches each time, it can still be a function.

3. **Outputs may repeat.**
   Different inputs can share the same output. That’s allowed.

4. **Not enough information?**
   A small table doesn’t prove something *is* a function for all inputs, but it **can** show when it is **not** a function.

**Example 1:** A function

| Input | Output |
| ----: | -----: |
|     2 |      7 |
|     3 |      9 |
|     2 |      7 |
|     4 |     11 |

The input 2 shows up twice, but with the **same** output (7). This table is consistent with a function.

**Example 2:** Not a function

| Input | Output |
| ----: | -----: |
|     1 |      4 |
|     1 |      5 |

The input 1 has **two different** outputs (4 and 5). Not a function.

:::{.gotcha title="Same output ≠ same input"}
It’s okay if **different inputs** give the **same output**. For example, two different temperatures could both “feel like” 75°F. That does **not** break the function rule.
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Function or not? Decide from each table."}
**(a)**

| Input | Output |
| ----: | -----: |
|    -1 |      3 |
|     0 |      1 |
|    -1 |      3 |
|     2 |      5 |

**(b)**

| Input | Output |
| ----: | -----: |
|     4 |     10 |
|     4 |     12 |
|     5 |     12 |

**(c)**

| Input | Output |
| ----: | -----: |
|     6 |      2 |
|     7 |      2 |
|     8 |      2 |
|    |        |

:::

:::{.answer title="Answers"}
(a) Function (repeated input has the same output).
(b) **Not** a function (input 4 maps to two different outputs).
(c) Function (different inputs share one output—allowed).
:::

***

### 2.5.3 - Evaluating Functions

Function notation is a handy way to describe expression evaluation.

Suppose we are asked to evaluate the expression $2x + 3$ when $x = 5$. We would do this:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2(\textcolor{red}{5}) + 3 &= 10 + 3 \\
&= 13
\end{aligned}
$$

Functions let us ask the same question with less writing. Instead we can just say "Find $f(5)$".

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\textcolor{red}{5}) &= 2(\textcolor{red}{5}) + 3 \\
&= 10 + 3 \\
&= 13
\end{aligned}
$$

**Example 3:** Evaluating functions

Let $g(x) = 3(x+4)$. Find $g(2)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(\textcolor{red}{2}) &= 3(\textcolor{red}{2}+4) \\
&= 3(6) \\
&= 18
\end{aligned}
$$

**Example 4:** Evaluating functions with negative numbers

Let $h(x) = -2(3x-1)+7$. Find $h(-2)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
h(\textcolor{red}{-2}) &= -2(3(\textcolor{red}{-2})-1)+7 \\
&= -2(-6 - 1) + 7 \\
&= -2(-7)+7 \\
&= 21
\end{aligned}
$$

:::{.real-world title="Programming: Functions everywhere"}
Programmers spend much of their time writing functions. A function has a name, takes inputs (also called parameters), and produces one output. The code behind any app you use often has hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of functions.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Evaluate $f(2)$ if $f(x) = 9 - 3x$"}
$f(2) = 9 - 3(2) = 9 - 6 = 3$
:::

***

### 2.5.4 - Simplifying Function Rules

Sometimes a rule is easier to use after you simplify it.

**Example 5:** Simplifying before evaluation

$$
p(x) = 4(x-2) + 3x
$$

First simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(x) &= 4x-8+3x \\
&= 7x-8
\end{aligned}
$$

Now evaluate at $x=5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(5) &= 7(5)-8 \\
&= 27
\end{aligned}
$$

:::{.think title="Why simplify the rule first?"}
A shorter rule makes evaluation quicker and reduces mistakes.
:::

Whenever possible, simplify before substituting—then you only have to do it once, no matter what input you plug in.

:::{.you-try title="Simplify $q(x) = 2(x+5) + 3x$. Then find $q(3)$."}
$q(x) = 5x+10$, so $q(3)=25$.
:::

***

### 2.5.5 - Function Evaluation in Real Life

Functions don’t just show up in math class—they model real situations. In science, functions describe how the world works. In everyday life, they help you predict costs or convert measurements. Below are two common examples.

***

**Example 6:** Cellphone data plan

A data plan charges a $\$50$ flat fee per month plus $\$0.10$ per Gb. How much will you pay if you use 80 Gb?

We can model the total cost with the function

$$
C(g) = 50 + 0.1g
$$

where $C$ is the total cost (dollars) and $g$ is data used (Gb).

Substitute $g=80$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(80) &= 50 + 0.1(80) \\
&= 50 + 8 \\
&= 58
\end{aligned}
$$

The total cost is **$\$58$**.

***

**Example 7:** Temperature conversion (°C → °F)

To convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit, use

$$
F(C) = \frac{9}{5}C + 32
$$

Find 25°C in Fahrenheit.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(25) &= \tfrac{9}{5}\cdot 25 + 32 \\
&= 45 + 32 \\
&= 77^\circ\mathrm{F}
\end{aligned}
$$

25°C = **77°F**

:::{.you-try-m title="How much will you earn?"}
You are paid $\$12$ per hour plus a $\$15$ bonus. You can represent your pay using

$$
P(h) = 12h + 15
$$

where $h$ is the number of hours worked and $P$ is your total pay.

How much do you make if you work for 40 hours?
:::

:::{.answer title="Answer"}
$P(40) = 12(40) + 15 = 480 + 15 = 495$
You make **$\$495$**.
:::
